why.correct: The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis: a single row of cells resting on the basement membrane, where the dermis bulges up into it. Its basal cells divide throughout life, and melanocytes and tactile cells sit among them.
options: The stratum spinosum lies just above the pinned layer and is 8 to 10 rows of cells thick, not a single row on the dermis.
Correct. The single deepest row, touching the dermis, is the stratum basale.
The stratum granulosum lies higher up, where cells flatten and fill with granules.
The stratum corneum is the surface layer of flat dead cells, at the opposite end of the epidermis.

why.correct: The stratum granulosum is the band of flattening cells speckled with granules: keratohyalin granules that bundle keratin, and lamellar granules that release lipids between the cells.
options: The stratum lucidum is the thin clear band just above, made of flat dead cells with no nuclei and no visible granules.
The papillary layer is the top of the dermis, below the whole epidermis, not a band of granule-filled cells within it.
Correct. Flattening cells full of small granules make the stratum granulosum.
The stratum spinosum is the thicker band of rounder cells below, which still have large nuclei and no granules.

why.correct: The stratum lucidum is a thin, clear band of flat dead cells filled with eleiden. It lies between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum, and only thick skin has it.
options: Correct. The clear band found only in thick skin is the stratum lucidum.
The stratum corneum is the much thicker surface layer above it, present in both thick and thin skin.
The stratum granulosum lies below the clear band and has visible granules and nuclei.
The papillary layer is part of the dermis, below the whole epidermis.

why.correct: The hypodermis, or subcutaneous layer, lies under the dermis. It is areolar and adipose tissue, which is why it looks like yellow fat lobules, and larger blood vessels run through it.
options: The dermis is the thick pink layer above the fat, made of dense connective tissue.
The epidermis is the thin surface layer at the top of the block.
The deep fascia is the dense sheet around the muscles, below the hypodermis; the block does not reach it.
Correct. The fatty layer beneath the dermis is the hypodermis.

why.correct: A tactile cell, also called a Merkel cell, sits in the stratum basale and presses against the flattened end of a sensory nerve fiber. It signals that nerve fiber when the skin is pressed.
options: A melanocyte also sits in the stratum basale, but it has long branches that pass pigment to keratinocytes and does not sit on a nerve fiber.
Correct. The cell paired with a nerve ending is the tactile (Merkel) cell.
Langerhans cells sit mainly in the stratum spinosum and take up foreign material; they are not paired with nerve fibers.
Basal cells are the dividing stem cells of the stratum basale; they are not linked to nerve fibers.

why.correct: Basal cells divide in the stratum basale. The new keratinocyte makes keratin in the stratum spinosum, forms granules and loses its nucleus in the stratum granulosum, passes through the clear stratum lucidum (present in the thick skin of the palm), and ends as a dead flat cell in the stratum corneum before it is shed.

The epidermis is avascular: its cells are fed by diffusion from capillaries in the dermis. A cut that stays in the epidermis reaches no vessel, so it does not bleed. It can still sting, because some nerve endings reach into the lower epidermis.
options: Correct. No blood vessels in the epidermis means a shallow cut does not bleed.
Keratin is a structural protein inside keratinocytes. It plays no part in stopping blood flow.
A paper cut makes no significant heat. The reason is where the cut stops, not how it seals.
The stratum corneum is dead keratin-filled cells. Clotting depends on platelets and proteins in the blood, which the epidermis does not contain.

why.correct: Basal cells are stem cells in the stratum basale. Each division leaves one stem cell in place and pushes the other up to become a keratinocyte, so the epidermis renews itself from the bottom.
options: Tactile cells pass touch signals to nerve fibers; they do not supply new keratinocytes.
Stratum corneum cells are dead. They have no nucleus and cannot divide.
Correct. The dividing stem cells of the epidermis are the basal cells.
Fibroblasts make the fibers of the dermis. They do not form epithelial cells.

why.correct: Five strata, a stratum lucidum and a very thick stratum corneum with no hair are the marks of thick skin, found on the palms, the soles and the palm side of the fingers and toes.
options: The upper back has the thickest skin overall because of its deep dermis, but its epidermis is thin skin with four strata and hair.
Correct. The sole is covered by thick skin.
The scalp is thin skin with a great deal of hair.
The eyelid has some of the thinnest skin on the body, with only four strata.

why.correct: Thick skin, on the palms and soles, has five strata including the stratum lucidum, a very thick stratum corneum, friction ridges from rows of dermal papillae, and no hair. "Thick" describes its epidermis, not its dermis.
options: Yes. Only thick skin has the clear stratum lucidum.
Yes. Rows of dermal papillae push thick skin into friction ridges, the fingerprints of the fingers.
No. Thick skin is hairless.
Yes. The stratum corneum of thick skin is many times deeper than in thin skin.
No. The skin of the upper back has a deeper dermis than the palm, yet it is thin skin. The name refers to the epidermis.

why.correct: People of all skin tones have about the same number of melanocytes at a given body site. Skin color depends on what those melanocytes make and pass on: in darker skin the melanosomes are larger, more heavily pigmented, more numerous in the keratinocytes and slower to be broken down.
options: Melanocyte numbers are similar across skin tones. The difference is in their melanin output and the melanosomes they deliver.
Melanocytes sit in the stratum basale in everyone, not in the dermis.
Correct. Melanosome size, pigment content and number set skin color.
Light skin still contains melanin, just less of it, often with more of the reddish pheomelanin.

why.correct: Melanocytes pass melanosomes along their branches to the keratinocytes of the epidermis. The pigment that makes a tan is in the keratinocytes, not in the dermis, which is why a tan fades as those cells are shed.
options: This step is right. UV damage to keratinocyte DNA starts the response.
This step is right. The damaged keratinocytes signal the melanocytes around them.
This step is right. Melanocytes build melanin from tyrosine with the enzyme tyrosinase.
This is the error. Melanin goes to the keratinocytes of the epidermis, not into the dermis.
This step is right. The melanin cap shades each nucleus from UV.

why.correct: Thin skin has four strata: basale, spinosum, granulosum and corneum. The stratum spinosum, where keratinocytes make keratin and are held together by desmosomes, lies just above the stratum basale.
options: The stratum lucidum lies between the granulosum and corneum, and only in thick skin.
Correct. The stratum spinosum comes next above the basale.
The papillary layer is the upper dermis, below the stratum basale, not inside the epidermis.
The reticular layer is the deep dermis, well below the epidermis.

why.correct: Lamellar granules release lipids into the spaces between cells, where they spread into sheets that seal the stratum corneum like mortar between bricks. Without that lipid seal, water escapes through the gaps between the dead cells, so the skin dries and loses water quickly.
options: Correct. The lipid sheets from lamellar granules are the main seal against water loss.
Keratin filaments are made in the stratum spinosum and bundled by keratohyalin, not by lamellar granules.
Tanning depends on melanocytes and melanin, which lamellar granules do not affect.
Basal cells lie below the stratum granulosum. A lipid defect higher up does not stop their division.

why.correct: The reticular layer is about 80% of the dermis. Its thick collagen bundles run in many directions, with elastic fibers among them, so it resists pulling from any direction.
options: The papillary layer is the thin upper part of the dermis, made of loose (areolar) tissue.
The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is areolar and adipose tissue, not part of the dermis.
The stratum spinosum is a layer of the epidermis, made of epithelial cells.
Correct. The thick, deep, dense irregular layer is the reticular layer.

why.correct: In each area the reticular layer's collagen bundles run mostly in one direction, the tension line. A cut parallel to them separates few bundles and is not pulled open by them, so its edges stay close and less scar tissue is needed.
options: Blood vessels are spread through the dermis in every direction, so no cut line avoids them all.
Correct. Cutting along the collagen keeps the edges together.
Removing a mole means cutting through the dermis. The direction of the cut, not its depth, gives the benefit here.
The dermal papillae are tiny bumps at the top of the dermis. Any cut crosses many of them.

why.correct: The hypodermis, or subcutaneous layer, is also called the superficial fascia. It is areolar and adipose tissue that ties the dermis loosely to the deep fascia over the muscles.
options: The deepest layer of the epidermis is the stratum basale. The hypodermis lies below the dermis, outside the skin itself.
That describes fascia around muscles, the deep fascia, which lies under the hypodermis.
Correct. Superficial fascia is an older name for the hypodermis.
Friction ridges are made by the dermal papillae of thick skin, at the top of the dermis.

why.correct: Melanin in the epidermis hides color changes from the blood beneath. The lips, gums, tongue and inside of the lower eyelid have little melanin and thin coverings over their blood vessels, so a bluish tint shows there first.
options: The upper back has thick dermis and normal melanin, so a color change from the blood is hard to see.
The forehead has the same melanin as the rest of the face, which masks the color of blood.
The skin over the knee is pigmented and often thickened, so it hides the color of blood.
Correct. Areas with little melanin show cyanosis best.

why.correct: Heat causes vasodilation of the small vessels of the dermis. More blood flows into the capillaries, and its red color shows through the epidermis as erythema.
options: Melanin production takes days to rise and gives a brown tan, not a quick red flush.
Carotene gives a slow, yellow-orange tint from diet, not a red flush after heat.
Less blood in the dermis would cause pallor, the opposite of redness.
Correct. Erythema is redness from more blood in the dermis.

why.correct: Carotene is a yellow-orange, lipid-soluble plant pigment. It collects in the stratum corneum and the fat of the hypodermis. The thick stratum corneum of the palms and soles holds the most, so they turn orange first. It is harmless and fades when the diet changes.
options: Correct. A diet rich in carotene tints the skin, most where the stratum corneum is thick.
Melanocytes make eumelanin and pheomelanin in response to UV and genes, not to diet, and they would not color only the palms and soles.
Vasodilation causes a red flush that comes and goes, not a lasting orange color on the palms and soles.
Too little oxygen in the blood causes a bluish color, cyanosis, not orange.

why.correct: Langerhans cells sit mainly in the stratum spinosum. Their branching arms spread between keratinocytes, and they take up microbes and other foreign material that enter the epidermis.
options: Melanin is made by melanocytes in the stratum basale, not by Langerhans cells.
The stratum corneum is dead cells; shedding happens as desmosomes between surface cells are broken down.
Collagen is made by fibroblasts in the dermis.
Correct. They sit in the stratum spinosum and take up foreign material.

why.correct: Each column has one melanocyte at the base, in the same place. What differs is the melanosomes: on the dark side they are darker and spread through many keratinocytes up toward the surface; on the light side they are pale and fewer.
options: Both columns show a single melanocyte at the base. Melanocyte numbers are about the same in all skin tones.
Correct. The melanosomes, and the pigment they deliver, differ.
Both columns show the same layers of keratinocytes.
In both columns the melanocyte sits at the bottom of the epidermis, on the dermis.

why.correct: Repeated rubbing slides the stiff upper epidermis back and forth over the layers beneath. The dermal papillae lock the epidermis to the dermis, so the living keratinocytes of the upper stratum spinosum tear apart first. Fluid from the dermis's capillaries seeps into the split and lifts a roof of stratum granulosum and stratum corneum.
options: The hypodermis is loosely attached and slides; rubbing tears the epidermis itself instead.
Correct. A friction blister is a split within the epidermis, in the upper stratum spinosum.
The dermal papillae grip the epidermis so firmly that the living epidermal cells above them tear apart first. Only some severe burns and blistering diseases split the skin at this junction.
Adipose tissue lies deep in the hypodermis, far below where rubbing splits the skin.

why.correct: The hair matrix is the layer of rapidly dividing cells in the bulb, just above the papilla. Its new cells are pushed upward, fill with hard keratin and die, forming the hair.
options: The hair papilla is the knob of connective tissue with capillaries beneath the matrix. It supplies the matrix but does not make the hair.
Correct. The dividing cells that make the hair form the hair matrix.
The inner root sheath lines the follicle around the hair; it is not the growing layer at the base.
The cortex is the middle layer of the hair itself, made of dead cells, not a layer of dividing cells in the bulb.

why.correct: The arrector pili is a small bundle of smooth muscle that runs from the side of the follicle up to the papillary dermis. When it contracts it pulls the hair upright and makes a goose bump.
options: The sebaceous gland is the lobed oil gland that opens into the follicle, not the slanting strip of muscle.
The inner root sheath lines the follicle right around the hair; it is not a strip of muscle outside the follicle.
Correct. The slanting strip of smooth muscle is the arrector pili.
The outer root sheath is part of the follicle wall, wrapped around the hair.

why.correct: The sebaceous gland is a lobed oil gland beside the follicle. Its cells fill with lipid and burst, and the sebum flows into the follicle and up onto the hair.
options: An eccrine sweat gland is a tight coil deep in the dermis with its own duct to a surface pore, not a lobed gland on the side of a follicle.
An apocrine sweat gland is a coiled tube that empties into a follicle higher up; the lobed shape here is an alveolar oil gland.
Ceruminous glands are found only in the ear canal.
Correct. The lobed gland emptying into the follicle is a sebaceous gland.

why.correct: The lunula is the white crescent at the base of the nail body: the visible part of the nail matrix. Its thick layer of cells hides the capillaries beneath, so it looks white.
options: Correct. The white crescent at the base of the nail is the lunula.
The free edge is the white rim at the tip of the nail, not the crescent at its base.
The eponychium is the thin band of skin lying over the base of the nail, just behind the lunula.
The hyponychium is the thickened skin under the free edge at the fingertip.

why.correct: The eponychium, also called the nail cuticle, is a thin band of stratum corneum that grows from the proximal nail fold onto the base of the nail body and seals the gap between them.
options: The hyponychium lies under the free edge at the other end of the nail.
The lateral nail folds run along the sides of the nail, not across its base.
Correct. The band over the nail's base is the eponychium, or cuticle.
The nail bed lies beneath the nail body and cannot be seen from above as a band of skin.

why.correct: An eccrine sweat gland is a coiled tube deep in the dermis with its own duct that winds up to a pore on the skin surface.
options: A sebaceous gland is lobed and empties into a hair follicle, not through a pore of its own.
Correct. A coiled gland with its own duct to a surface pore is an eccrine sweat gland.
An apocrine sweat gland's duct empties into a hair follicle, not onto the skin surface.
The hair bulb is the swollen base of a follicle, around the hair papilla.

why.correct: The cortex is the thick middle layer of tightly packed, keratin-filled cells. It holds most of the melanin and gives the hair its strength.
options: The medulla is the loose central core, often absent in fine hairs.
The cuticle is a single thin layer of shingle-like cells on the outside.
Correct. The cortex holds most of the pigment and strength.
The hair papilla is connective tissue at the base of the follicle, not a layer of the hair.

why.correct: During pregnancy, high hormone levels keep extra scalp follicles in anagen. After the birth those levels fall abruptly, and the held-over follicles enter catagen and telogen at the same time. Telogen lasts about 3 months; when those follicles start a new anagen, the new hairs push the old club hairs out together. The follicles are intact, so the hair regrows.
options: The matrix cells are not destroyed; the follicles are resting. The hair grows back once they re-enter anagen.
Sebum oils the hair but does not hold it in the follicle, and loss of sebum would not cause shedding three months later.
The arrector pili raises a hair by tilting it; it cannot pull hairs out.
Correct. Follicles pushed into the resting phase together shed together about three months later.

why.correct: Chemotherapy stops the rapidly dividing matrix cells of anagen follicles, so hairs stop growing and fall out within weeks. Because about 85 to 90% of scalp follicles are in anagen, the loss is widespread. The follicles survive, so hair regrows after treatment.

variables.name: Cell division in the matrix of anagen follicles
variables.why: The drug kills or stops rapidly dividing cells, and anagen matrix cells are among the fastest-dividing cells in the body.

variables.name: Rate of hair lengthening
variables.why: Hair grows only from matrix cell division, so when division stops the hair stops lengthening and its base becomes thin and weak.

variables.name: Number of hairs shed
variables.why: The weakened hairs of anagen follicles break or fall out, and most scalp follicles are in anagen, so shedding rises sharply.

variables.name: Number of melanocytes in the skin of the arm
variables.why: Melanocytes in the skin divide rarely, so a drug aimed at rapidly dividing cells leaves their number about the same over a few weeks.

why.correct: In anagen, matrix cells divide and the hair grows. In catagen, division stops, the follicle shrinks and the base of the hair becomes a club. In telogen, the club hair rests. When the next anagen begins, a new hair grows up beneath the old one and pushes it out, and the cycle repeats.

Apocrine sweat glands, in the armpits, groin and around the nipples, empty into hair follicles, start working at puberty, and make a thicker secretion with proteins and lipids that bacteria turn into body odor. Eccrine glands are the densest on palms and soles and the ones that release heat.
options: Yes. Apocrine ducts open into hair follicles above the sebaceous glands.
Yes. They become active at puberty.
No. The palms and soles have no hair follicles and are packed with eccrine glands instead.
Yes. Proteins and lipids make apocrine secretion thicker than eccrine sweat.
No. Heat loss through sweat is the job of eccrine glands; apocrine glands respond mainly to emotional stress.

why.correct: Apocrine secretion contains proteins and lipids. Bacteria living on the skin feed on them, and the small, strong-smelling molecules they release are body odor. Deodorants work largely by slowing those bacteria.
options: Sebum is on skin everywhere, yet odor comes mainly from areas with apocrine glands.
Eccrine sweat is mostly water and salt and has no smell of its own.
Correct. Bacteria acting on the proteins and lipids in apocrine secretion make the odor.
Apocrine glands release their product mainly by exocytosis, and in any case the fresh secretion has no smell.

why.correct: The secreting coil makes a watery fluid like protein-free plasma. As it flows up the duct, duct cells take back sodium and chloride. The faster the flow, the less time for that, so more salt stays in the sweat that reaches the skin.
options: Correct. Less time in the duct means less salt taken back, so fast sweat is saltier.
Apocrine glands respond to emotion, not heat, and they are few; heavy sweating in a race comes from eccrine glands.
Sebaceous glands make an oily lipid product, not salt.
The coil's fluid starts at about the same salt level whatever the rate. What changes with flow is how much the duct takes back.

why.correct: In holocrine secretion the whole cell bursts and becomes the product, so the gland uses up cells as it secretes. It depends on stem cells dividing to replace them. Block that division, and fewer cells fill with lipid and burst, so sebum output falls.
options: Correct. A holocrine gland needs a steady supply of new cells.
The gland would run short of cells to fill and burst, so output falls, not rises.
Sebum is made of lipids and cell debris; blocking cell division reduces the amount, not the water content.
Sweat glands release by exocytosis and do not use up their cells, so this drug's effect on sebaceous stem cells would not reduce sweat.

why.correct: Shaving cuts the hair shaft at the surface. The shaft is dead and the matrix sits deep in the bulb, untouched, so the hair's width, color and growth rate do not change. The cut end is blunt instead of tapered, which feels stubbly, and short new hair has not yet been lightened by sun.
options: The matrix is deep in the follicle and receives no signal from a cut at the surface.
The cuticle is part of each hair and is made fresh by the matrix; shaving the shaft does not change the new hair's layers or pigment.
Correct. Only dead shaft is removed, so the new hair is the same; it only feels coarser.
The growth cycle is set inside the follicle, not by cutting the shaft above the skin.

why.correct: The nail matrix, the thickened layer of dividing cells under the nail root, makes the nail. Its new cells fill with hard keratin, die, and are pushed forward.
options: The nail bed lies under the nail body and the plate slides over it; it does not make the nail.
Correct. The nail matrix makes new nail.
The hyponychium is thickened skin under the free edge; it seals, but does not make, the nail.
The eponychium is a band of stratum corneum over the nail's base; it does not make the nail plate.

why.correct: The nail matrix, under the nail root beneath the proximal nail fold, makes the nail. Scarring there changes the plate the matrix produces, leaving it ridged or split for good. The nail bed only supports the plate as it slides forward, so injury there usually heals without a lasting deformity.
options: The nail bed supports the plate; the matrix, not the bed, makes it.
Nails grow from the matrix at their base, not from the free edge.
The lunula is only the visible front of the matrix at the base of the nail; it does not cover the nail bed.
Correct. Damage to the matrix changes the nail it makes.

why.correct: The arrector pili is a small bundle of smooth muscle. It contracts involuntarily when nerve signals triggered by cold or fear reach it, raising the hair.
options: Correct. Smooth muscle, contracting involuntarily.
You cannot raise goose bumps at will the way you move a skeletal muscle. The arrector pili is smooth muscle.
Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart wall.
The arrector pili contracts; connective tissue cannot.

why.correct: Duct cells take back sodium and chloride from the fluid; they do not add them. That is why sweat on the skin is less salty than the fluid first made in the coil, especially when sweat flows slowly.
options: This step is right. The coil makes a fluid like plasma with its proteins removed.
This step is right. The duct carries the fluid up through the dermis and epidermis.
This is the error. The duct removes sodium and chloride; it does not add them.
This step is right. Each eccrine duct opens at its own pore.
This step is right. Sweat is mostly water, with some salt, potassium and lactate.

why.correct: A hair's maximum length is its growth rate times the length of anagen. Eyebrow hairs grow only about half as fast as scalp hairs, but scalp follicles stay in anagen for years and eyebrow follicles for only a few months, so the hair enters catagen and telogen, and is shed, while still short.
options: Uncut eyebrows reach the same short length whether or not they are rubbed; the limit is set in the follicle.
Every growing hair needs a matrix; without one, eyebrows would not grow at all.
Eyebrow hairs are terminal hairs with a normal cortex.
Correct. A short anagen phase limits how long the hair gets.

why.correct: The nail plate is clear dead keratin with no pigment. The pink is blood in the dense capillaries of the dermis beneath the nail bed. Pressing squeezes the blood out; releasing lets it flow back in, and the speed of return reflects blood flow to the fingertip.
options: The nail body is clear, which is why the color beneath it shows through.
Correct. The pink is blood in dermal capillaries under the nail bed.
Melanin would give a brown color that does not blanch when pressed.
Carotene is yellow-orange and does not change with pressure.

why.correct: The shaft is the part of the hair above the skin surface; the root is the part inside the follicle, below the surface. Both are dead keratinized cells; only the matrix at the base is alive and growing.
options: Correct. The shaft is above the surface and the root below it.
Both the shaft and the root are dead keratin-filled cells. The living cells are in the matrix of the bulb.
Both parts are keratinized cells. The connective tissue at the base is the papilla, not the root.
Growing and resting are phases of the whole follicle over time, not parts of one hair.

why.correct: Despite the name, apocrine sweat glands release their product mainly by exocytosis, the merocrine mode. The name is historical. Many exams still give them as the example of apocrine secretion; the milk-making glands of the breast are the clear case of true apocrine release.
options: Holocrine secretion, where the whole cell bursts, is how sebaceous glands work.
Correct. The evidence shows mainly merocrine release.
This is the historical claim that gave the glands their name, and the answer many exams expect, but microscopy shows mainly exocytosis.
Sweat glands are exocrine: their product leaves through a duct, not into the blood.

why.correct: Exercise raises heat production. The temperature loop responds with vasodilation in the dermis, which warms the skin surface, and with eccrine sweating. In dry air the sweat evaporates, so heat loss by evaporation rises and body temperature is held near its set point.

variables.name: Heat produced by her muscles
variables.why: Working skeletal muscle breaks down far more fuel, and most of that energy is released as heat.

variables.name: Dermal blood flow
variables.why: Warm-sensitive endings signal the brain's temperature control center, which sends signals that widen the vessels of the dermis.

variables.name: Skin surface temperature
variables.why: More warm blood flowing through the dermis carries heat to the skin surface.

variables.name: Eccrine sweat output
variables.why: The control center signals the eccrine sweat glands to secrete.

variables.name: Heat lost by evaporation
variables.why: More sweat is on the skin, and dry air lets it evaporate quickly, each liter removing about 580 kcal.

why.correct: Cold triggers the "too cold" half of the loop. Vasoconstriction lowers dermal blood flow, so the skin cools and less heat is carried to the surface. The arrector pili contract, shivering raises heat production, and sweating stops.

variables.name: Dermal blood flow
variables.why: Cold-sensitive endings signal the brain's temperature control center, which narrows the vessels of the dermis.

variables.name: Skin surface temperature
variables.why: Less warm blood reaches the skin, and wind carries heat from the surface, so the skin cools.

variables.name: Arrector pili contraction (goose bumps)
variables.why: The control center's nerve signals make the arrector pili muscles contract, raising the hairs.

variables.name: Heat production by skeletal muscle
variables.why: Shivering: rapid involuntary contractions of skeletal muscle release nearly all their energy as heat.

variables.name: Eccrine sweat output
variables.why: With the body cooling, the control center stops the signals that make eccrine glands secrete.

why.correct: When the air is hotter than the skin, radiation and convection add heat, and evaporation is the only way to lose it. Humidity slows evaporation, so more sweat drips off uselessly, less heat is lost, and body temperature climbs even though the worker is sweating hard.

variables.name: Rate at which sweat evaporates
variables.why: Humid air already holds a lot of water vapor, so water on the skin turns to vapor more slowly.

variables.name: Sweat dripping off unevaporated
variables.why: Sweat that cannot evaporate builds up on the skin and runs off.

variables.name: Heat lost by evaporation
variables.why: Only sweat that evaporates removes heat; dripping sweat removes almost none.

variables.name: Internal body temperature
variables.why: At 36 °C the air is hotter than the skin, so evaporation is the only route of heat loss; with it reduced, heat builds up.

why.correct: Heat moves from warmer to cooler. When the surroundings are hotter than the skin, radiation, conduction and convection all carry heat into the body. Evaporation only ever removes heat, so it is the one route left.
options: With surroundings hotter than her skin, radiation carries heat toward her, not away.
Air hotter than her skin conducts heat into her.
Moving air hotter than her skin adds heat as it flows past.
Correct. Evaporation removes heat whatever the air temperature, as long as the air is not saturated.

why.correct: Heat removed = volume evaporated × 580 kcal/L = 0.8 × 580 = 464 kcal.
options: 725 comes from dividing 580 by 0.8. Multiply the volume by the heat per liter instead.
Correct. 0.8 L × 580 kcal/L = 464 kcal.
580 kcal is the heat for a full liter; only 0.8 L evaporated.
46 kcal is ten times too small: 0.8 × 580 is 464, not 46.4.

why.correct: Evaporation is the only route when the air is hotter than the skin. Volume = heat ÷ 580 kcal/L = 696 ÷ 580 = 1.2 L per hour, and more if some drips off.
options: 0.8 comes from dividing 580 by 696, the wrong way round.
4.0 L would remove about 2,300 kcal, more than three times the heat he makes.
1.0 L removes only 580 kcal, less than the 696 kcal he makes.

why.correct: The cooling comes from water turning into vapor, which takes energy from the skin. In humid air sweat evaporates slowly, so much of it drips off still liquid and carries away almost no heat. Lots of visible sweat can mean poor cooling.
options: Correct. Evaporation, not the amount of sweat, sets the cooling.
A film of water does not trap heat; the problem is that it is not evaporating.
Sweating and wide dermal vessels go together in heat; sweating does not stop blood flow.
The heat the glands produce is tiny compared with the heat evaporation could remove.

why.correct: UVB opens a ring of 7-dehydrocholesterol, making previtamin D3, which body warmth turns into vitamin D3. The liver then makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main form in the blood, and the kidneys make the active hormone, which raises calcium and phosphate absorption in the intestine.
The liver adds the first hydroxyl group, making 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main circulating form. The kidneys then add the second.
options: Correct. The liver makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and blood-sugar hormones; it plays no part in activating vitamin D.
The stratum corneum is dead cells; vitamin D is made in the living keratinocytes below it, and it is activated elsewhere.
The intestine is where the active hormone acts, absorbing calcium; it is not an activating step.

why.correct: He has rickets. Winter sun at high latitude gives little UVB, dark skin absorbs more of it, and he stays indoors, so his skin makes little vitamin D; breast milk alone supplies little. Too little vitamin D means too little active hormone, so his intestine absorbs little calcium and phosphate. New bone stays soft, and his legs bow under his weight.
options: Melanin does not harm bone. It lowers vitamin D synthesis by absorbing UVB, which is only one link in the real chain.
Correct. This is the chain that leads to rickets.
Bone hardening depends on calcium absorption, not on warmth from sunlight.
The problem is too little calcium reaching the bone, not too much.

why.correct: A normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D level shows the skin and liver steps are working. The final step, adding the second hydroxyl group to make the active hormone, happens in the kidneys, so failing kidneys make too little of it and calcium absorption falls. She needs the active hormone itself as a drug.
options: If the skin step had failed, and she ate little vitamin D, her 25-hydroxyvitamin D would be low, not normal.
This conversion also happens in the skin, before the liver step; a normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D level shows it is working.
The liver's product is 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and its level is normal.
Correct. The kidneys make the active hormone, and hers are failing.

why.correct: Once enough previtamin D3 has built up, further UV light converts it and vitamin D3 into inactive molecules instead of more vitamin D3, so synthesis levels off. Too much vitamin D comes only from supplements.
options: A tan takes days to develop and only partly blocks UVB; it is not what caps vitamin D synthesis.
The liver's step is not what limits the amount the skin makes.
Correct. Extra UV turns the precursors into inactive products.
Cells make cholesterol and 7-dehydrocholesterol continuously; supply is not what caps the amount.

why.correct: Lamellated corpuscles sit deep in the dermis and hypodermis. Their many layers pass on fast changes in pressure and filter out steady pressure, so they respond best to deep pressure and fast vibration.
options: Correct. Deep, fast vibration is the lamellated corpuscle's specialty.
Free nerve endings mainly sense pain, temperature and itch.
Tactile cells sense steady light pressure and texture near the surface, not fast vibration.
Hair follicle endings sense a hair bending; the fork presses on skin and bone.

why.correct: Tactile corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae, just under the epidermis, and are most numerous in hairless skin such as the fingertips and lips. They respond to light touch and slow vibration.
options: The stratum corneum is dead cells with no nerve endings.
The hypodermis holds the deep lamellated corpuscles, not the tactile corpuscles.
Correct. They sit in the dermal papillae.
Endings wrapped around follicles are the hair follicle endings, a different kind.

why.correct: The onion-like structure deep in the dermis is a lamellated (Pacinian) corpuscle: a nerve ending wrapped in many layers, which senses deep pressure and fast vibration.
options: Tactile corpuscles are small and sit high in the dermal papillae, just under the epidermis.
Correct. The large, layered capsule deep in the dermis is a lamellated corpuscle.
The coil of an eccrine sweat gland is a tangle of tubing with a duct rising to a pore, not a layered capsule.
The arrector pili is a slanting strip of smooth muscle attached to a hair follicle.

why.correct: The acidic surface slows many microbes, shedding removes those stuck to surface cells, the lipid sheets seal the gaps between dead cells, and Langerhans cells take up microbes that get into the epidermis. Dermal blood flow and tactile cells serve heat exchange and touch.
options: Yes. Many harmful microbes grow poorly at the skin's acidic pH.
Yes. Microbes stuck to surface cells are shed with them.
No. Dermal blood flow mainly sets heat loss; it lies below the epidermis and does not keep microbes out of it.
Yes. The lipid sheets close the gaps between dead cells.
Yes. They take up microbes that get past the surface.
No. Tactile cells signal light touch.

why.correct: The barrier of the stratum corneum is made of lipid sheets between dead cells. Lipid-soluble (hydrophobic) molecules dissolve into that lipid and slowly pass through; water-soluble molecules cannot cross it easily. Skin-patch drugs are chosen to be lipid soluble.
options: Sweat flows outward, from the glands to the surface, so it cannot carry drugs inward.
The skin's pH of about 5 is only mildly acidic and does not destroy most drugs.
Correct. Lipid solubility lets a drug cross the lipid barrier.
Size matters less than whether the molecule can dissolve in the lipid sheets that fill the spaces between the cells.

why.correct: Water conducts heat about 25 times faster than air, so wet clothes draw heat from the skin quickly, and the wind blows over them and evaporates the water, which removes more heat. Conduction, convection and evaporation all rise together.
options: Radiation depends on the temperature difference between skin and surroundings, which is the same for both hikers.
Correct. Conduction through water plus evaporation drain heat fast.
Cold wet skin makes shivering stronger, not weaker.
Cold water on the skin narrows the dermal vessels; the heat loss comes from the water itself.

why.correct: In cold, the dermal vessels narrow (vasoconstriction). That keeps warm blood deeper in the body, cools the skin surface and shrinks the gradient that drives heat loss. Widening them would lose heat faster.
options: This step is right. The skin is the first to cool.
This step is right. Cold-sensitive endings are the sensors.
This step is right. The control center compares input with the set point and sends out commands.
This is the error. Dermal vessels narrow in the cold; they widen in heat.
This step is right. Shivering makes heat.

why.correct: Many texts say skin vessels widen in heat only because the steady signal that narrows them weakens. In hairy skin such as the forearm, active widening by nerves accounts for most of the rise. Withdrawal of the narrowing signal is the main mechanism only in the hairless skin of the palms, soles and lips.
options: The finding confirms that dermal blood flow rises in heat.
Correct. Active widening, not just withdrawal, drives most of the rise in hairy skin.
The finding depends on the vessels having a nerve supply; it confirms it.
Sweating and vasodilation do happen together in heat; the finding does not contradict that.

why.correct: Her skin gives off infrared rays to any cooler surface, even one she is not touching. The cold glass absorbs more than it returns, so she loses heat on that side by radiation although the air is warm.
options: Conduction needs contact; she is not touching the window.
The air around her is warm, so convection is not what chills her on that side.
Evaporation does not depend on which side a cold surface is on.
Correct. Radiation carries heat to cooler surfaces without contact.

why.correct: Alkaline soap raises the skin's normally acidic pH, and repeated washing strips the lipid sheets from the stratum corneum. Microbes grow better at a higher pH, and cracks and lost lipid open routes into living tissue.
options: Correct. A higher pH and lost lipids weaken the barrier against microbes.
Melanin protects against UV, not microbes, and washing does not affect it.
Dermal blood flow lies below the epidermis and does not change the skin surface that keeps microbes out.
Tactile corpuscles sense touch; damaging them would dull sensation, not invite infection.

why.correct: Free nerve endings are bare, branching tips of sensory nerve fibers in the lower epidermis and throughout the dermis. They respond to painful stimuli, warmth and cold, and itch.
options: Tactile corpuscles sense light touch and slow vibration.
Lamellated corpuscles sense deep pressure and fast vibration.
Correct. Free nerve endings handle pain, temperature and itch.
Tactile cells sense steady light pressure and texture.

why.correct: Vitamin D synthesis needs UVB to reach 7-dehydrocholesterol in the keratinocytes. Window glass blocks nearly all UVB, and in winter at high latitude the low sun sends little UVB through the atmosphere in the first place.
options: Winter sunlight still contains some UV, mostly the longer-wavelength kind; it is UVB that is scarce, and glass removes what is left.
The liver's step does not depend on activity.
Less melanin would let more UVB through, not less, and melanin does not run out.
Correct. Little UVB arrives in winter at that latitude, and the glass stops what does.

why.correct: Across the integumentary, cardiovascular and urinary systems: a large burn removes the skin's barrier and makes capillaries leak body-wide. Water evaporates from the wound and plasma leaks into the tissues, so blood volume and blood pressure fall, heart rate rises to compensate, and urine output falls. That is why large burns need large volumes of fluid in the first day.

variables.name: Water lost by evaporation from the skin
variables.why: The burned skin has lost its stratum corneum and lipid seal, so water evaporates freely from the wound surface.

variables.name: Volume of interstitial fluid
variables.why: Heat damage and chemical messengers make capillaries leaky, so water, salts and proteins move from the plasma into the spaces between cells, and the tissue swells.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Fluid leaves the vessels into the tissues and out through the burned surface faster than it is replaced.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: With less blood volume, less blood returns to the heart and less is pumped into the arteries.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The body responds to the falling blood pressure by speeding the heart.

variables.name: Urine output
variables.why: Low blood pressure reduces blood flow to the kidneys, so they make less urine.

why.correct: Front of the trunk = 18%; one whole upper limb = 9%. 18 + 9 = 27%.
options: 18% is the front of the trunk alone; the arm adds another 9%.
Correct. 18 + 9 = 27%.
36% is the whole trunk, front and back; only the front is burned.
45% would be the whole trunk plus one arm.

why.correct: Back of the trunk = 18%. Each whole lower limb = 18%, so both = 36%. 18 + 36 = 54%.
options: 36% counts only the two legs and leaves out the back.
45% counts each leg as 9% plus the whole trunk; each whole leg is 18%, and only the back of the trunk is burned.
72% counts the whole trunk, front and back, instead of the back only.

why.correct: Each whole lower limb is 18%, front and back together. The front of one leg is half of that, 9%. Both fronts: 9 + 9 = 18%.
options: 9% is the front of one leg; both legs are burned.
36% is both whole legs, front and back; only the fronts are burned.
Correct. 9 + 9 = 18%.
27% has no basis here: it would be one whole leg plus the front of the other.

why.correct: In an infant the head and neck count 18%, not 9%, because the head is a larger share of a baby's body. Front of trunk = 18%. 18 + 18 = 36%.
options: 27% uses the adult value of 9% for the head and neck, which underestimates an infant's burn.
18% counts only one of the two burned regions.
45% adds an extra 9% that has no burned region to match it.

why.correct: Only partial- and full-thickness burns count. The sunburn is superficial (red, painful, no blisters) and leaves the barrier intact, so it is left out. The blistered arm is partial-thickness: 9%.
options: 27% adds the superficial sunburn, which is not counted.
18% is the sunburned back alone, which does not count.
Correct. Only the arm's 9% counts.
36% is the whole trunk; neither the burns nor the rule support it.

why.correct: The chart gives each lower limb as 18% and the genital area as 1%. 18 + 1 = 19%.
options: Correct. 18 + 1 = 19%.
10% treats the lower limb as 9%, the value for an upper limb.
18% is the lower limb alone and leaves out the genital area.
37% counts both lower limbs.

why.correct: Blisters, a moist red surface and severe pain mark a superficial partial-thickness burn: the epidermis and papillary layer are damaged, but capillaries and nerve endings deeper in the dermis survive. Fluid leaking from injured capillaries lifts the dead epidermis into blisters.
options: A superficial burn damages only the epidermis and does not blister.
Correct. Blisters with severe pain mean a superficial partial-thickness burn.
A full-thickness burn is dry, leathery and painless in its center, because its nerve endings are destroyed.
A fourth-degree burn reaches muscle, tendon or bone, far deeper than a brief scald.

why.correct: A full-thickness burn destroys the whole dermis with its nerve endings, so its center is painless, white and leathery. The partial-thickness burn around it still has living nerve endings and capillaries, so it hurts and blisters. Painlessness here means the deepest damage.
options: A superficial burn is red and painful, not white, leathery and numb.
Partial-thickness burns hurt and blister; a numb, leathery area has lost its nerve endings, which means full thickness.
Correct. The numb center is the deepest part of the burn.
A red, blistered, painful ring has living nerve endings, which rules out full thickness; a burn does not heal from its center outward within hours.

why.correct: Hair follicles and sweat gland ducts are lined by epithelium that reaches deep into the dermis, below a partial-thickness burn. Those cells divide and spread out across the wound bed, and the islands grow together into new epidermis. A full-thickness burn destroys them, so it cannot regrow epidermis from within.
options: Fibroblasts make collagen and scar tissue; they do not become epithelial cells.
Fat cells lie below the dermis and do not form epidermis.
Melanocytes make pigment; they do not supply keratinocytes.
Correct. The epithelium of follicles and ducts regrows the surface.

why.correct: Bleeding stops first, with a clot and scab. Inflammation then brings cells that clear debris. In the rebuilding stage, capillaries and fibroblasts form granulation tissue while epithelial cells cover it and the edges contract. Finally, over months, remodeling reorganizes the collagen into a mature scar.

A wound with separated edges and lost tissue heals by secondary union. It fills from the bottom with granulation tissue, its edges are pulled together by wound contraction, and it closes over weeks, leaving a wider scar.
options: Primary union needs edges held close together, as in a stitched cut; this wound is left open.
A wound through the dermis with lost tissue fills partly with collagen, so it scars.
Correct. Open wounds heal by secondary union.
Whether a wound heals by primary or secondary union depends on whether its edges are together, not on the scab.

why.correct: Granulation tissue is the moist, pink, grainy tissue that fills a healing wound: new capillary loops (the grains) with fibroblasts laying down collagen among them. It bleeds easily because of its many new vessels.
options: Dead keratinized cells in lipid sheets make the stratum corneum, not granulation tissue.
Mature scar forms later, in remodeling, as most of the new capillaries disappear.
Fat is not part of granulation tissue.
Correct. New capillaries plus collagen-making fibroblasts.

why.correct: A keloid is a scar that keeps growing beyond the original wound's edges, because fibroblasts go on making excess collagen during remodeling. Earlobes are a classic site, and keloids are more common in darker skin.
options: Correct. A scar growing beyond the wound's edges is a keloid.
Granulation tissue is soft, pink and moist, fills a wound in its first weeks, and does not grow beyond the wound.
A callus is flat, thickened stratum corneum from friction, not a firm raised lump after a wound.
Basal cell carcinoma is a pearly bump on sun-exposed skin, usually in older adults, not a growing scar at a piercing.

why.correct: A pearly, shiny bump with fine surface vessels and a central sore on sun-exposed facial skin of an older person with years of sun is typical of basal cell carcinoma, the most common skin cancer. It grows slowly and rarely spreads.
options: Melanoma usually appears as a dark, uneven, changing patch, not a pearly bump.
Squamous cell carcinoma is usually a scaly red patch or crusted sore; the pearly surface with fine vessels points to a basal cell cancer.
Correct. This is the classic look of basal cell carcinoma.
A keloid is an overgrown scar after a wound, not a cancer.

why.correct: Asymmetry, an irregular border, several colors, a diameter over about 6 mm, and change over time (evolving) all raise concern for melanoma. An evenly colored spot that has not changed for years is reassuring.
options: Yes. Asymmetry is the A of ABCDE.
No. A single even color is reassuring; several shades would be concerning.
Yes. An irregular border is the B.
Yes. Larger than about 6 mm is the D.
Yes. Change in size or color is the E, evolving, and it is the most important sign.
No. A spot stable for decades is unlikely to be a melanoma.

why.correct: Melanoma starts in melanocytes, which can break loose early, pass through the dermis into vessels and spread to lymph nodes and distant organs. Basal cell carcinoma rarely spreads, so it is common but rarely deadly.
options: Correct. Early spread is what makes melanoma dangerous.
Melanoma can appear anywhere, including easily seen skin; that is why skin checks work.
Thin melanomas removed early are usually cured.
Most melanomas appear as new spots rather than in an existing mole.

why.correct: Sustained pressure over a bony area, higher than the pressure inside the capillaries, flattens them. Blood stops flowing, the cells run out of oxygen and nutrients, and they begin to die by necrosis. Redness that does not blanch is the first sign of a pressure injury.
options: Correct. Compressed capillaries starve the tissue.
A mattress is not hot enough to burn skin; the damage comes from pressure.
Infection can follow once skin breaks down, but the first damage is from lost blood flow.
The heel is thick skin with no hair and no sebaceous glands.

why.correct: A blackhead is a follicle plugged with sebum and shed keratinocytes and open at the surface. Where the plug meets the air, its lipids and melanin change and darken. Scrubbing does not remove it and can irritate the skin.
options: The dark color is not dirt; it forms in the plug itself where it meets the air.
There is no bleeding in a blackhead.
The follicle bacteria involved in acne are not what color a blackhead.
Correct. The exposed plug darkens on contact with air.

why.correct: In albinism, melanocytes are present in normal numbers but make little or no melanin, because of faulty genes for melanin-making proteins such as tyrosinase. In vitiligo, the immune system destroys the melanocytes in the affected patches, so they are missing.
options: Melanocytes are present in albinism; they just make little or no melanin.
Correct. Albinism: melanocytes with little or no melanin. Vitiligo: melanocytes gone.
This reverses the two conditions.
Both conditions leave the skin with little or no melanin, so neither sample would be normal.

why.correct: Repeated friction makes the basal cells divide faster, and the stratum corneum thickens into a callus. It protects the skin beneath and thins again if the rubbing stops.
options: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and does not thicken from friction on the surface.
The reticular layer does not thicken into a hard surface patch.
The papillary layer does not become hard; the hard surface is dead keratinized cells.
Correct. A callus is thickened stratum corneum.

why.correct: Histamine, prostaglandins and other messengers released after a burn make capillaries more leaky, not less. Water, salts and proteins leave the plasma for the interstitial fluid, which is one of the two main reasons blood volume falls.
options: This step is right. The burn removes the skin's barrier.
This step is right. Without the barrier, water evaporates freely from the wound.
This is the error. The messengers make capillaries more leaky, so fluid leaves the vessels.
This step is right. Fluid lost to evaporation and to the tissues lowers blood volume.
This step is right. Lower blood volume means less blood returning to the heart and lower pressure.

why.correct: Leaky capillaries let water, salts and proteins pass from the plasma into the interstitial fluid. That fluid is still in the body but no longer in the vessels, so blood volume and blood pressure fall.
options: Correct. Plasma moving into the tissues is the step that lowers blood volume.
Urine output falls, not rises, as blood pressure falls.
The leak lets fluid and proteins out; red blood cells mostly stay in the vessels.
Sweat glands in burned skin are destroyed, and sweat is not the main loss after a burn.

why.correct: Keratohyalin proteins bundle keratin into the tough cells of the stratum corneum. When one is faulty, the layer is weaker: it loses water, dries and cracks, and lets irritants reach living cells. An overactive immune response to those irritants then causes the itching and inflammation of eczema.
options: Keratohyalin proteins have nothing to do with melanin, and eczema is not a pigment disorder.
Correct. A weak stratum corneum is the barrier fault in eczema.
The fault is in how keratin is bundled, not in how fast basal cells divide.
Eczema skin is dry, not oily; sebum output is not the problem.

why.correct: When skin is stretched faster than the dermis can grow, as in a growth spurt or pregnancy, collagen and elastic fibers of the reticular layer tear and thin. The skin over them flattens into lines that fade from red to silvery white but never fully recover.
options: Loss of melanocytes in patches is vitiligo.
A thickened stratum corneum is a callus.
Plugged follicles are the start of acne.
Correct. Stretch marks are torn and thinned dermal fibers.
